paper_title: CARTBench: Rubric-Based Evaluation of Shopping Advice for Complex and Ambiguous Requests with Timelines

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language model (LLM) shopping assistants now recommend products in multi-turn conversations. However, reliable evaluation faces Data scarcity and Difficulty Standardizing Criteria. To address these obstacles, we introduce CARTBench for CART (Complex and Ambiguous Requests with Timelines). For Data scarcity, we curate cases from real commercial shopping needs across 17 retail domains, pairing timestamped dialogue with 1,603 product records. For Difficulty Standardizing Criteria, we develop case-specific rubrics guided by Ideal Response Principles, distilled from excellent replies manually selected from successfully completed orders. These principles also guide Principle-Guided CART Prompting, our structured recommendation strategy. The experimental benchmark contains 1,328 expert-annotated criteria across Core, Excellence, and Safety. To answer the CART question, we evaluate 7 flagship commercial API models, including GPT-6.1-Sol and Claude-Opus-5, and 35B+ parameters open-weight models. In the first full-suite evaluation under the frozen rubrics, 3 of 10 models exceed 90% on Core, while none exceeds 45% on Excellence. Therefore, we identify an understanding-to-execution gap between required behavior and high-quality purchase advice. To examine these limitations, we diagnose shared failures in product evidence and unresolved needs, linked to changing requirements and decisive unknowns. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Da1yuqin/CARTBench.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: LLM shopping assistants help shoppers choose products for stated or implicit needs (Mukherjee et al., 2025; Dammu et al., 2025; Dhole et al., 2025). *Corresponding authors: Yongliang Shen (syl@zju.edu.cn); Boyuan Pan (daoxuan@xiaohongshu.com). 1 Figure 1: CART case: an expired gift deadline (Timelines), one-bag limit (Complexity), and an unknown hospital list and feeding plan (Ambiguity). Matched colors link reply excerpts to their checks. However, shopping needs can be complex or unclear and may expire over time (Figure 1). This raises the question: How well can LLMs handle Complex and Ambiguous Requests with Timelines (CART)? Existing shopping benchmarks do not explicitly report timeline inputs, and none credits replies that keep unconfirmed preferences and conditions open  (Table 1)  . Without timelines, an evaluation cannot tell whether advice follows need that has already expired; without credit for open unknowns, it cannot separate lucky guess from justified conditional answer. However, establishing reliable CART evaluation faces two main obstacles. 1) Data scarcity: access to real commercial data is difficult. Further, identifying complex and ambiguous needs in confidential commercial conversations requires costly Benchmark WebShop (Yao et al., 2022) EComAgentBench (Du et al., 2026) ShoppingComp (Tou et al., 2025) Shopping Reasoning Bench (Fan et al., 2026) MMShopBench (Hao et al., 2026) PACEShopc (Lyu et al., 2026) RealWorldShopc (Yang et al., 2026) CARTBench (ours) Case design Evaluation Hard Dialogue Timeline Validity Intent Evidence Fit Unknowns Per-case Safety a a Table 1: Shopping benchmark comparison. Hard selection: difficult-request screening; Dialogue: prior turns or clarification; Timeline: timestamps or elapsed time. Need validity: historical needs still apply; Intent accuracy: goal understanding; Evidence check: product-claim support; Fit basis: user and product evidence justify suitability; Unknowns preserved: unconfirmed needs are not assumed; Per-case: manually tailored reply rubrics; Safety: recommendation risks. Shaded : covered; : absent; : partial; : unreported. : product-choice scores; no direct goal assessment. Shopping Reasoning Bench: separate Hard subset. No public code/data link located. ShoppingComp checks fit to stated needs; conditional fit under unknown user needs is not explicit. annotation. In addition, 2) Difficulty Standardizing Criteria: different products and user needs require different checks. For example, even within the same retail domain, such as clothing, recommend an item of clothing can imply different needs. These can depend on gender, age, style, occasion, and the intended gift recipient. Timeline information can also reveal expired needs; gift intended for an earlier date may already have been given. shared checklist cannot capture these differences, yet criteria written case by case without common standard are hard to keep consistent across cases. To address these obstacles, we introduce CARTBench, benchmark grounded in real shopping needs for evaluating CART advice. For Data scarcity, we curate CART cases from real commercial shopping needs. For each case, timestamped dialogue retains changed needs and unanswered questions. Through stratified sampling, CARTBench covers 17 common retail domains and pairs dialogue with 1,603 product records. For Difficulty Standardizing Criteria, we develop case-specific rubrics guided by Ideal Response Principles. Experts distill these principles from excellent replies manually selected from successfully completed orders, and instantiate them as case-specific rubrics. The principles keep criteria consistent across cases, and the rubrics adapt them to each case. The experimental benchmark contains 1,328 criteria across Core, which checks required behavior, Excellence, which rewards high-quality advice beyond it, and Safety, which checks case-specific risks. Models receive the same principles, but not the rubrics, through Principle-Guided CART Prompting. To answer the CART question, we evaluate 7 flagship commercial API models, including GPT6.1-Sol and Claude-Opus-5, and 35B+ parameters open-weight models. Under the frozen evaluation protocol, the first full-suite evaluation shows that 3 of 10 models exceed 90% on Core, while none exceeds 45% on Excellence. Therefore, we identify an understanding-to-execution gap. Here, meeting Core requirements does not ensure high-quality guidance for purchase decisions. To examine these limitations, further diagnosis reveals shared failures in product evidence and unresolved needs, linked to changing requirements and decisive unknowns. Our contributions are: We introduce CARTBench, which evaluates CART advice on real commercial shopping needs with timestamped dialogue, product evidence, and case-specific rubrics. We propose Ideal Response Principles, distilled from excellent replies, which keep casespecific rubrics consistent across cases and guide Principle-Guided CART Prompting. We identify an understanding-to-execution gap. Further diagnosis reveals shared failures across models in product evidence and unresolved needs.

sections.title: 2.1 Shopping Recommendation
sections.content: Use cases and implicit needs guide recommendations without requiring exact product attributes 2 Figure 2: CART workflow with selected travel-case turns. An undecided destination (Ambiguity) and linked power requirements (Complexity) motivate Core, Excellence, and Safety checks. Highlights distinguish request stages and clarity. Ideal Response Principles guide rubrics and prompting; rubrics remain hidden from the shopping model. The reply is illustrative; empty boxes denote checks. An expert reviews labels; N/A means not applicable. (Mukherjee et al., 2025; Dammu et al., 2025; Dhole et al., 2025). Personalization draws on elicited or inferred preferences (Lucas de Carvalho et al., 2025; Kostric et al., 2025; Kook et al., 2025), profiles, and external knowledge (Chien et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025). Related benchmarks assess preference adherence (Zhao et al., 2025b,a; Narasimhan and Narasimhan, 2026), user states, and dialogue consistency (Li et al., 2026; Sirdeshmukh et al., 2025). However, data scarcity limits evaluation of complex and ambiguous commercial needs. To address this gap, we curate CART cases based on experts screening for interacting or unclear needs. This enables targeted CART evaluation, addressing the shortage of real commercial cases.

sections.title: 2.2 Shopping Evaluation
sections.content: Shopping evaluations assess actions and product selection (Yao et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2026; Lyu et al., 2025). Extensions test hidden preferences (Du et al., 2026) and retrieval (Hao et al., 2026). Advice assessment adds factual comparisons (Vedula et al., 2023) and expert rubrics (Tou et al., 2025; Fan et al., 2026). Evidence-grounded checks support judge evaluation (Lyu et al., 2026) and rubric design (Mei et al., 2026). RealWorldShop tests changing, ambiguous needs in simulated sessions (Yang et al., 2026). However, CART evaluation requires case-specific checks with consistent standards. To overcome this limitation, we develop case-specific rubrics guided by our Ideal Response Principles. This enables systematic CART evaluation, aligning common standards with case-specific needs.

sections.title: 3.1 CART Problem Formulation
sections.content: To assess how well LLMs meet needs and support decisions, we formalize CART advice. CART 4 denotes Complex and Ambiguous Requests with Timelines. Requirements can interact, change, or expire. Preferences or decisive facts may remain unknown. Even everyday clothing and gift purchases depend on recipients, preferences, occasions, and deadlines. Advice must therefore follow active needs and justify choices without guessing unknowns. Criterion outcomes guide diagnosis of failures in product evidence and unresolved needs. We assess the current reply, excluding upstream elicitation and purchase outcomes. To distinguish active from outdated needs, each case supplies timestamped dialogue history and current request q. Cached product evidence and current message time complete the input (Figure 2). Relative dates retain their original message-time anchors. Model uses Ideal Response Principles to generate reply from x: = (h, q, E, t), = (x). We next construct these inputs and rubrics.

sections.title: 3.2 Data Collection
sections.content: To address data scarcity and standardize checks, we construct case inputs and expert-designed rubrics in four steps. Figure 3 shows how case-specific rubric distinguishes stronger and weaker replies to the same request. Step 1: Sources and Case Selection. To capture CART needs, experts screen real commercial requests for interacting requirements, changes, unclear goals, and decisive unknowns. To limit evaluation costs, rather than evaluating large dataset at substantial time and financial cost, we use stratified sampling to select 169 representative cases across 17 retail domains. At official list prices, one complete 169-case evaluation costs less than US$24 per API model for inference and judging, enabling cost-effective large-scale model selection. Cases span eight intents; dates and intervals distinguish active, expired, and unconfirmed historical needs. Coverage. To document coverage, we summarize shopping targets and overlapping requirement groups in Figure 4. The outer ring subdivides mechanisms and combines rare groups. Evaluation retains the original eight mechanisms. The rings Figure 4: Case coverage across shopping targets (inner) and overlapping requirements (outer). Shares use cases and caserequirement-group pairs, respectively. show separate distributions, not intersections. Unequal group sizes reflect stratified selection, not shopping traffic. Step 2: Product Evidence Collection. To compare models on fixed evidence, we cache records for the selected needs. An internal product search platform supplies 1,603 records. Internet searches confirmed the products could be found online. The records contain titles and available prices, specifications, and descriptions. Missing fields remain missing. Retrieval establishes neither user endorsement nor suitability. Step 3: Ideal Response Principles. To standardize checks, experts distill four Ideal Response Principles. The source comprises excellent replies manually selected from successfully completed orders. To protect privacy, we do not share these replies. These principles guide case-specific rubrics and Principle-Guided CART Prompting. Ideal Response Principles (Summary) 1. Address the current purchase decision. 2. Follow active needs; preserve unknowns. 3. Ground claims and explain trade-offs. 4. Give clear and useful decision help. Step 4: Case-Specific Rubric Design. To tailor checks, experts adapt shared principles to each cases dialogue and evidence. The frozen experimental rubrics contain 1,328 criteria after expert review. Each criterion checks one observable behav5 ior and accepts supported alternatives (Mei et al., 2026). The criteria form three business-oriented tiers: = RCore RExcellence RSafety. (2) Each criterion belongs to one tier. Core covers goal alignment, requirement adherence, uncertainty preservation, evidence fidelity, plan validity, and decision support. These criteria guide Evidence-Grounded Rubric Judging, our prompt for evidence-linked labels (Section 3.4). The comparison in Figure 3 complements Figure 2 by separating product choice from reply quality. Other supported products or combinations can pass the applicable checks. Open-ended needs have no unique ground-truth product set, so we omit productmatching F1. We next generate replies from the constructed inputs.

sections.content: To compare advice under shared conditions, we give models without browsing or rubric access. Principle-Guided CART Prompting. To ground recommendations, we apply shared principles to need analysis, product comparison, and justification. Replies may compare products, prioritize purchases, or offer conditional alternatives. Clarifying questions should affect decisions. Unresolved conditions remain open. We next assess these replies against the hidden rubrics.

sections.content: We first identify shared Core failure modes and locate the same errors across scenarios. Separately, we assess plan validity after resolved need and evidence checks pass.

F2: Shopping Uncertainty Collapse treats unknown preferences, possessions, purchase needs, or scenario conditions as settled. All three modes occur in every evaluated model, although cases differ. Thus, grounded shopping advice requires supported product facts and justified links to user needs. Diagnosis scope. sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: CARTBench pairs timestamped dialogue and product evidence with case-specific rubrics, guided by Ideal Response Principles and Principle-Guided CART Prompting. Expert-confirmed results reveal an understanding-to-execution gap and shared failures in evidence, suitability, and unresolved needs. Even replies passing all resolved need and evidence checks can fail plan checks.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: First, although we cover common shopping scenarios such as gifting and travel clothing, specialized Figure 6: Scenario reply rates for context-state drift (F1), premature need resolution (F2), unsupported product claims (F7), and unjustified suitability inference (F8). Cells use equal model and case weights; groups overlap. Decisive unknowns expose more evidence and fit errors than premature need resolution. In decisive-unknown scenarios, both F7 and F8 occur more often than F2. Thus, preserving unknowns also requires bounding product and suitability claims. Evidence checks ask whether product claims follow from the supplied records. Fit checks ask whether those supported attributes warrant recommendation for the current user. Figure 7 shows the same profiles. We next test plan validity after need and evidence checks pass. 8 needs merit further study. Examples include historically accurate costumes for museum reenactments and equipment for extended polar expeditions. Second, although we assess recommendations under changing needs, feedback from actual product use may introduce new requirements. How advice should adapt across longer purchase, return, and replacement cycles merits further study.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: CARTBench is provided solely for academic research and evaluation. Our cases are grounded in real commercial shopping needs. Product information is supplied by an internal product search platform. Internet searches were used only to confirm that corresponding products could be found online. Third-party content remains subject to the original rights and applicable terms. Experts annotate requirements from visible dialogue and retrieved evidence. Evaluation rewards grounded explanations and respects user choice.
